evidence_quotes.quote: We present an overview of the distribution of bird diversity in the forests of the canal area based on 10 years of inventories.

Our primary objectives were to (1) map the distribution of avian diversity throughout canal-corridor forests, particularly with respect to two common correlates of diversity, rainfall and forest tract size
Do legally protected lands preserve the region’s forest birds at present?
We studied birds in 18 forest patches along the canal corridor (Fig. 1).
Species richness was well predicted by annual rainfall (n = 18 sites, r2 = 0.40, p = 0.0048) and, separately, by area (ha; n = 18 sites, r2 = 0.77, p < 0.0001).

criterion_notes.c1: Fails Criterion 1. The study examines the spatial distribution and conservation of terrestrial forest bird diversity across 18 forest patches in the Panama Canal corridor, not household or community water or sanitation service access (mentioning only in passing that the forests serve as the water supply for the canal).
criterion_notes.c2: Fails Criterion 2 under the active 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type reading: the paper does not examine any legal, administrative, regulatory, or governance rule-type mechanism governing water or sanitation service access (such as eligibility screening, administrative burden, documentation/tenure requirements, tariffs, discretion, enforcement, or utility regulation). Under the plain literal wording of Criterion 2 ('Examines a legal, administrative, institutional, regulatory or governance factor'), the paper descriptively compares forest bird diversity across legally protected national parks/monuments versus unprotected or ARI-zoned 'protection forest' tracts for biodiversity conservation, which is an environmental land-use designation unrelated to water or sanitation services; even if counted under the plain wording, the study is still excluded because it fails Criteria 1 and 4.
criterion_notes.c3: Satisfies Criterion 3. Empirical ecological study based on 10 years (1993-2002) of field bird inventories across 18 forest patches, supplemented by Audubon/Christmas Bird Count records and analyzed via multiple regression.
criterion_notes.c4: Fails Criterion 4. Outcomes are avian species richness and presence/distribution of resident and migratory forest bird species across forest tracts; no water or sanitation service access, connection, availability, reliability, quantity, affordability, or exclusion outcome is reported.
criterion_notes.c5: Satisfies Criterion 5 within its ecological domain: unit of analysis/sample is 18 lowland forest patches (and their bird communities) in central Panama; exposures/correlates are forest patch area, annual rainfall, and national legal protection status; outcome is forest bird species richness; study design is a multi-year observational ecological inventory with cross-sectional multiple-regression analysis.
criterion_notes.c6: Satisfies Criterion 6. Full text is in English (with a Spanish abstract).

study_design: Observational ecological inventory (1993-2002) with cross-sectional multiple-regression analysis across 18 forest patches
population_and_sample: Avian communities across 18 lowland tropical moist forest patches (21 ha to 15,020 ha) in the Panama Canal corridor, Republic of Panama
exposure: Forest tract area (ha), annual rainfall (mm), and national park/protected area legal designation
outcome: Forest bird species richness and distribution of rare/resident/migratory bird species across forest patches
rationale: Excluded under E01 (Wrong topic). This is a conservation biology and ornithology paper mapping avian species richness across 18 forest tracts in the Panama Canal corridor as a function of forest area, rainfall, and protected-area status. It does not study household or community water or sanitation service access (c1=no), does not examine any rule-type mechanism governing water or sanitation access (c2=no), and reports no water or sanitation access outcomes (c4=no). Both the narrow 2026-10-13 Criterion 2 reading and the plain wording yield exclusion.
